title: Future and polite requests
objectives: I can read and write every word of this unit and explain each accent from the stress rule.
I can talk about the future with ir plus infinitive, the present and the simple future, and explain when each is used.
I can make polite requests and express wishes with gostaria, poderia, deveria and seria, and explain why the conditional sounds polite.
I can give suggestions and advice with Por que você não, Que tal and Se eu fosse você.
I can express probability with deve ser and será que, and make an appointment by phone.

vocabulary.note: Pre-vi-ZÃO. The ending ão is stressed on the last syllable by default, so only the tilde is written, and it also marks the nasal sound. A single s between two vowels is said z. It comes from prever, to foresee (pre- before, ver to see), so a previsão do tempo is the weather forecast.

example.pt: A previsão é de chuva para amanhã.
example.en: The forecast is for rain tomorrow.
example.literal: The forecast is of rain for tomorrow.

vocabulary.note: Fu-TU-ro. The stress is on the second to last syllable, the default for an ending in o, so no accent is written. The final o is said u.

example.pt: No futuro, quero morar perto do mar.
example.en: In the future, I want to live by the sea.
example.literal: In-the future, I-want to-live near of-the sea.

vocabulary.note: Em is a nasal vowel, because a vowel followed by m or n in the same syllable is nasal. Breve is BRE-vi: the final unstressed e is said i. The phrase means in a short time, which is why the English word brief is its literal sense.

example.pt: Em breve vou receber o resultado.
example.en: I will get the result soon.
example.literal: In brief I-go to-receive the result.

vocabulary.note: It is de plus aqui plus the preposition a. In daqui the qu before i is the k sound with a silent u, and the stress is on the last syllable, the default for i. It counts a period of time forward from now. The mirror image for the past is há dois anos, two years ago.

example.pt: Daqui a dois anos eu me formo.
example.en: In two years I graduate.
example.literal: From-here to two years I me form.

vocabulary.note: Pro-va-vel-MEN-te. The adjective provável has a written accent because it ends in l but is stressed on the second to last syllable. In an adverb in -mente the main stress is on men, so the adjective's written accent is dropped. The ending -mente works like English -ly.

example.pt: Provavelmente vai chover à tarde.
example.en: It will probably rain in the afternoon.

vocabulary.note: Ser-TE-za: c before e is the s sound, and the stress is on te, the second to last syllable, the default for a. It is also the usual confident yes to a question or an offer.

example.pt: Com certeza eu vou à festa.
example.en: I will definitely go to the party.

vocabulary.note: SO-nho. Nh is one sound, like ny in canyon. The verb is sonhar.

example.pt: Meu sonho é abrir uma padaria.
example.en: My dream is to open a bakery.

vocabulary.note: Used both for the dream you have asleep (Sonhei com você, I dreamed about you) and for the one you hope for. The preposition is com, not de.

example.pt: Sonho com uma casa perto do mar.
example.en: I dream of a house by the sea.
example.literal: I-dream with a house near of-the sea.

vocabulary.note: A false friend. Realizar means to make real, to carry out: realizar um sonho is to fulfill a dream, and realizar um evento is to hold an event. English to realize, meaning to become aware, is perceber or dar-se conta. Re-a-li-ZAR is stressed on the last syllable, the default for r, and the initial r is the strong h-like sound.

example.pt: Quero realizar o meu sonho.
example.en: I want to fulfill my dream.

vocabulary.note: Conditional of gostar de, to like. Gos-ta-RI-a has the stress on ri and no accent, but the nós form gostaríamos moves the stress to the third to last syllable and needs the accent. In cafes and shops Brazilians often say eu queria instead, which is not followed by de.

example.pt: Eu gostaria de agendar uma consulta.
example.en: I would like to book an appointment.
example.literal: I would-like of to-schedule a consultation.

vocabulary.note: Conditional of poder, the standard polite request form. Po-de-RI-a is stressed on ri, so no accent; the nós form is poderíamos.

example.pt: Você poderia me ajudar, por favor?
example.en: Could you help me, please?
example.literal: You would-be-able me to-help, for favor?

vocabulary.note: Conditional of dever, which basically means to owe. Devia is the more casual spoken form. De-ve-RI-a is stressed on ri, so no accent.

example.pt: Você deveria descansar mais.
example.en: You should rest more.

vocabulary.note: Conditional of ser. Se-RI-a is stressed on ri, so no accent.

example.pt: Seria ótimo viajar com você.
example.en: It would be great to travel with you.

vocabulary.note: A formal alternative to por favor, used with strangers and in service situations. G before e is the zh sound, and the stress is on le (gen-ti-LE-za).

example.pt: Por gentileza, aguarde um momento.
example.en: Please wait a moment.

vocabulary.note: Formal synonym of esperar, related to guardar, to keep or guard. Gu before a is different from gu before e: the u is pronounced, so it is a-GWAR-dar. The stress is on the last syllable, the default for r.

example.pt: Aguarde na linha, por favor.
example.en: Please hold the line.

vocabulary.note: The grave accent on à is the crase: the preposition a fused with the article a. Dis-po-zi-ÇÃO is stressed on the last syllable, the default for ão, so only the tilde is needed. The s between two vowels is said z, and the ç is said s. Shops and professionals say Estou à disposição or Estamos à disposição to offer help.

example.pt: Estou à disposição para qualquer dúvida.
example.en: I am at your disposal for any questions.
example.literal: I-am at-the disposition for any doubt.

vocabulary.note: Re-ser-VAR, stressed on the last syllable, the default for r. The s between two vowels is said z, and the initial r is the strong h-like sound.

example.pt: Gostaria de reservar uma mesa para quatro.
example.en: I would like to reserve a table for four.

vocabulary.note: Used for a medical, dental or professional appointment; for other meetings use reunião. Con-SUL-ta: the on is a nasal vowel, and an l at the end of a syllable is said like w.

example.pt: Tenho uma consulta com a dentista na terça.
example.en: I have an appointment with the dentist on Tuesday.
example.literal: I-have a consultation with the dentist on-the Tuesday.

vocabulary.note: Ho-RÁ-ri-o. The h is silent. The ending io counts as two syllables, so the stress is on the third to last syllable, which no ending predicts and which therefore always takes an accent. Open a, so acute. It comes from hora, hour.

example.pt: Tem horário disponível amanhã de manhã?
example.en: Is there a time slot available tomorrow morning?
example.literal: Has time-slot available tomorrow of morning?

vocabulary.note: From agenda, a diary or planner. G before e is the zh sound and en is nasal: a-zhen-DAR, stressed on the last syllable, the default for r.

example.pt: Posso agendar uma consulta para sexta?
example.en: Can I book an appointment for Friday?

vocabulary.note: Dis-po-NÍ-vel. The stress is on the second to last syllable, but an ending in l expects the last, so an accent is written. The plural disponíveis keeps it, because an ending in is also expects the last syllable. The form is the same for masculine and feminine.

example.pt: Esse horário não está disponível.
example.en: That time slot is not available.

vocabulary.note: Dever basically means to owe. Must and probably are extensions of that idea. Followed by ser, estar or ter, deve expresses a guess about the present.

example.pt: Deve ser difícil morar sozinho.
example.en: It must be hard to live alone.

vocabulary.note: Será is the future of ser, and it introduces a question the speaker asks themselves. Se-RÁ has its stress on the last syllable, but an ending in a expects the second to last, so the acute accent is written.

example.pt: Será que vai chover amanhã?
example.en: I wonder if it will rain tomorrow.

vocabulary.note: Also o mês que vem and o ano que vem. Vem is the singular of vir, he, she or it comes; the plural vêm carries a circumflex which only distinguishes it in writing.

example.pt: Vamos marcar para a semana que vem.
example.en: Let's schedule it for next week.
example.literal: Let's mark for the week that comes.

vocabulary.note: Fosse is the imperfect subjunctive of ser, the form for imagined situations; a later note explains it. The ss between vowels is said s, and the final unstressed e is said i: FOS-si.

example.pt: Se eu fosse você, aceitaria o emprego.
example.en: If I were you, I would accept the job.

dialogues.title: Booking a dental appointment
dialogues.context: Gustavo calls a dental clinic to book an appointment. The receptionist, Fernanda, answers.

dialogues.title: Dreams for the future

lines.en: Henrique, where do you see yourself in five years?
lines.literal: Henrique, where you see-yourself from-here to five years?

lines.speaker: Henrique
lines.pt: Com certeza ainda aqui em São Paulo. Meu sonho é abrir uma padaria.

lines.speaker: Paula
lines.pt: Uma padaria? Seria ótimo! Você faz um pão de queijo incrível.

lines.speaker: Paula

lines.speaker: Henrique

lines.speaker: Paula

dialogues.title: At the hotel front desk
dialogues.context: Beatriz is staying at a hotel and needs to leave early for the airport. She asks the receptionist, Otávio, for help. In a hotel, o café (literally the coffee) means the breakfast served in the morning.

lines.literal: Good night. I would-like of to-ask a favor. You would-be-able me to-call a taxi for tomorrow early?

lines.pt: Com prazer. A que horas?

lines.literal: With pleasure. At what hours?

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: the words and verb endings of this unit
grammar.explanation:
Nothing in this unit's spelling is new. Every accent and every unusual letter follows a rule from the first three lessons, and this note shows those rules at work on the new words so that you can read and write them instead of memorizing them. Two questions solve almost every word. First, where is the stressed syllable, and does it agree with the default for the word's ending? Words ending in a, e or o (with or without s) and in am, em or ens are stressed on the second to last syllable, and most other endings, including l, r, z, i, u, is, us and ão, are stressed on the last syllable. When the stress disagrees with the default, an accent is written on the stressed vowel: acute for an open vowel, circumflex for a closed one. Second, what do the neighboring letters say about how a letter is pronounced? The letters c and g, the pairs qu and gu, a vowel followed by m or n, and the digraphs nh and rr are all decided by what surrounds them.

The biggest group of accents comes from the two new verb tenses, and one idea explains all of them: the endings place the stress in different spots, and the accent follows the stress. The simple future is built by adding an ending to the whole infinitive (falar plus ei gives falarei). In falarei the stress is on the ending ei, a diphthong, and the default for ei is the last syllable, so no accent is needed. In falará the stress is on the final a. An ending in a is expected to be stressed on the second to last syllable, so stress on the last syllable breaks the default and takes an acute accent: fa-la-RÁ. The same reasoning gives será, terá, fará and começará, and it is the same reasoning that gave você its circumflex. In falarão the ending ão is stressed on the last syllable by default, so the tilde, which marks the nasal sound and the stress, is enough. In falaremos (fa-la-RE-mos) the stress is on the second to last syllable, the default for os, so there is no accent, just as the present falamos needs none.

The conditional endings -ia, -ia, -íamos and -iam are the endings of the imperfect of comer and abrir from the imperfect unit, and they are written by the same logic. In gostaria the stress is on ri (gos-ta-RI-a), the second to last syllable, which is the default for an ending in a, so there is no accent; the i and the a are two separate syllables (a hiatus), not a diphthong. In gostaríamos (gos-ta-RÍ-a-mos) the extra syllable pushes the stress to the third to last syllable, which no ending predicts, so an accent is required, exactly as in comíamos and éramos. The í only marks the stress, because i has a single sound. The same logic gives poderíamos, deveríamos and seríamos.

Several nouns and adjectives of the unit are proparoxytones, stressed on the third to last syllable, and these always take an accent: clínica, horário, salário, negócio, dúvida, ótimo, trânsito. Endings written io and ia count as two syllables, so ho-RÁ-ri-o and ne-GÓ-ci-o are stressed on the third to last. Other words break the default by being stressed on the second to last syllable although their ending predicts the last: disponível (dis-po-NÍ-vel) and incrível end in l, and táxi ends in i. The plural disponíveis keeps the accent, because an ending in is also expects the last syllable. The adjective provável has the same accent as disponível for the same reason, but in provavelmente the accent disappears. The ending -mente turns an adjective into an adverb, like English -ly, and it was once a separate word, so the adverb has its main stress on men (pro-va-vel-MEN-te) and the written accent of the adjective is dropped, as in fácil and facilmente.

The letters follow the rules of the sounds lesson. The ending ão is stressed on the last syllable by default, so previsão, reunião, confirmação and recepção need only the tilde, which marks the nasal sound. A single s between two vowels is said z (previsão is pre-vi-ZÃO), while ss is said s (compromisso, posso, fosse). Ç is the s sound before a, o or u (confirmação, disposição, começará). C before e or i is s (certeza, cedo, cinco), and g before e or i is zh (gentileza, agendar, mensagem). Qu before e or i is the k sound with a silent u (daqui, queijo, Henrique). Gu before e keeps the g hard with a silent u, which is why chegar becomes chegue in the imperative (chegue quinze minutos antes). Gu before a is different: the u is pronounced, so aguardar is a-GWAR-dar. Nh is one sound like ny in canyon (sonho, dinheiro), rr is the strong h-like sound (sorriso), a lone h is always silent (horário), and x in táxi is ks. An l at the end of a syllable is said like w (consulta is con-SUW-ta), and a vowel followed by m or n in the same syllable is nasal (em breve, consulta, mensagem). A final unstressed e is said i (breve, fosse) and a final unstressed o is said u. In recepção the p is pronounced.

Two spellings come from the 2009 reform in the second lesson: voo (vo-o, two syllables, without the old circumflex) and ideia (i-DEI-a, without the old acute on the open ei of a paroxytone). The accents on até, já, amanhã and também follow the same procedure as everything else: find the stress, read the default for the ending, compare. Use the table as a checklist, and when a new word has an accent, do not ask whether to memorize it; count the syllables, find the stress and compare it with the default.

grammar.title: The future: ir plus infinitive, the present and the simple future
grammar.explanation:
Portuguese has three ways to talk about the time after now, and they do different jobs. First, ir plus infinitive, from the plans unit: a conjugated form of ir (to go) followed by the infinitive, so vou falar is literally I-go to-speak, the same structure as English I am going to speak. It is the ordinary spoken way to state plans, intentions and predictions: Vou falar com ele, Vai chover amanhã. Second, the simple present, for things already scheduled, as in English (The train leaves at eight): O voo sai às oito, Amanhã eu viajo. Third, the simple future: one word with a special ending, falarei. Simple here means that the tense is a single word, in contrast with the two-word vou falar.

English has no simple future. Its will is a separate helper word, called an auxiliary verb (a verb that helps another verb express tense or mood, like will, do and have), placed before the main verb. Portuguese fuses the helper into the verb as an ending. This is not a coincidence: the Portuguese future was built from the infinitive plus the present tense of haver (to have), so falar hei, literally I-have to-speak, wore down into falarei. That history explains two facts about the form. The endings are attached to the whole infinitive, not to the stem (the part left when you remove -ar, -er or -ir), so falar, comer and partir keep their -r: falarei, comerei, partirei. And the endings are the shrunken present of haver: -ei (from hei), -á (há), -emos (hemos) and -ão (hão). Everyday Brazilian speech uses four verb forms (eu, você with ele, ela and a gente, nós, and vocês with eles and elas), so there are four endings; tu, where it is used, takes -ás (falarás).

The rule has no exceptions except three verbs whose infinitive is shortened before the ending: fazer becomes farei, dizer becomes direi and trazer becomes trarei. The syllable ze dropped out long ago, and the shortened stems far-, dir- and trar- are what the endings attach to (the same stems return in the conditional). All other verbs keep the full infinitive, including the ones that are irregular in the present: serei, terei, irei, estarei, poderei, saberei, verei, virei. Pôr gives porei; the circumflex of pôr existed only to tell it from the word por (by), and porei has no such twin. Note the pair verei (I will see) and virei (I will come): the infinitives ver and vir differ by one vowel and so do their futures.

The uses follow from the forms. In everyday speech the simple future is much rarer than vou plus infinitive, and it sounds formal, written or solemn. You will meet it in news, weather forecasts, contracts, formal announcements and promises: A reunião começará às nove, O prefeito falará hoje à noite, Eu prometo que farei isso. In the dialogues, the clinic receptionist says Enviaremos uma mensagem (we will send), the formal voice of an institution, and the hotel receptionist says chamarei and deixarei, a formal promise to a guest. Among friends the same promises would be Vou chamar and Vou deixar. One trap: English uses the present after when and if (When I arrive, If it rains). Portuguese uses a different form there, the future subjunctive, which comes later, so do not translate those clauses with the simple future.

To place an event a number of days or years from now, use daqui a plus the period: Daqui a cinco minutos eu saio. Daqui is de (from) plus aqui (here), so daqui a dois anos is literally from-here to two years, and the verb is in the present or in vou plus infinitive. In very formal writing an object pronoun can be inserted inside the future form, as in dar-lhe-ei (I will give him). You will see this in formal documents but almost never hear it.

grammar.title: The conditional for politeness and wishes
grammar.explanation:
The conditional names what would happen, or what one would do, if some condition held. English builds it with the auxiliary would (I would go, you would like). Portuguese again fuses the helper into the verb, this time as the infinitive plus the endings -ia, -ia, -íamos and -iam. These are the same endings as the imperfect of comer and abrir, so there is only one new idea: as in the future, the ending is added to the whole infinitive, not to the stem. Gostar becomes gostaria, poder becomes poderia, dever becomes deveria, ser becomes seria. The same three verbs are shortened as in the future: fazer gives faria, dizer gives diria and trazer gives traria. The technical name is futuro do pretérito, future of the past, and it reveals the second job of the form: a future seen from a point in the past. Ele disse que viria means He said he would come: at the moment of speaking in the past, his coming was still in the future. Colloquially the imperfect takes over here too: Ele disse que vinha.

The job you need most at this level is politeness. A plain want, Quero um café, states your will as a fact and leaves no room to refuse. Eu gostaria de um café presents the wish as a hypothetical, a situation that would be pleasing, and a hypothetical is easier to decline politely. In both languages, the further the verb form stands from plain fact, the softer the request (I want, I would like). Você poderia me ajudar? is softer than Você pode me ajudar?, because poderia asks about the possibility instead of demanding the act. Deveria means should and gives advice more gently than deve, must. The literal sense of dever is to owe, so deve is you owe it, a debt, and deveria is you would owe it, a milder claim. Seria is would be, used in hypotheticals and polite judgments: Seria ótimo, Seria melhor esperar. Remember that gostaria needs de before a noun or an infinitive (gostaria de um café, gostaria de reservar), while queria does not.

In casual speech Brazilians often replace the conditional with the imperfect: Eu queria um café, Você podia me ajudar?, Você devia descansar. The imperfect gives the same distance from plain fact, because it is the tense that does not say the action was completed or asserted. Literally queria is I wanted, and the wanting is placed at a remove from the present moment. Both forms are polite and natural; gostaria is a little more formal than queria.

Mind the English word would, which has two jobs. If would can be replaced by used to, it is a past habit, and Portuguese uses the imperfect: When I was a child, I would play outside is Quando eu era criança, eu brincava na rua, never brincaria. If would describes an imagined situation, a polite wish or a future seen from the past, Portuguese uses the conditional.

grammar.title: If I were you: se plus fosse, and the conditional
grammar.explanation:
A conditional sentence has two clauses. A clause is a group of words built around its own verb. The if-clause states the condition (Se eu fosse você) and the main clause states the result (eu aceitaria o emprego). Everything depends on whether the condition is real or imagined. A real condition (If it rains, I stay home) uses a form you will study later, the future subjunctive. An imagined condition, one that is contrary to fact, uses the pattern of this note: in the if-clause, the imperfect subjunctive; in the main clause, the conditional.

The subjunctive is a mood, the way a verb shows how the speaker regards the event (see the grammar map in the third lesson). The indicative states facts; the subjunctive is used for what is imagined, wished for or doubted. English has almost lost its subjunctive, but a trace survives in If I were you. Nobody says If I was you in careful English, because the speaker is not you, and were marks that the condition is imagined. Portuguese does the same thing with a complete, regular set of forms. The whole imperfect subjunctive is taught in a later unit, so here you need only one form: fosse, the imperfect subjunctive of ser. It is built from the preterite, and ser and ir share one preterite (fui, foi), so fosse serves for both verbs: Se eu fosse você means if I were you, and Se vocês fossem ao Rio means if you went to Rio.

The pattern is therefore Se eu fosse plus the person, then the result in the conditional: Se eu fosse você, eu aceitaria o emprego. The two clauses use two different verb forms because they do two different jobs: fosse creates the imagined world, and the conditional says what would happen in it. That is why the main clause does not use the simple future (eu aceitarei), which would present the result as something you expect to happen. In casual speech the main clause is often in the imperfect: Se eu fosse você, eu aceitava.

The forms of fosse change with the subject. The nós form, fôssemos, has its stress on the third to last syllable (FÔS-se-mos), so it needs an accent, and the circumflex shows the closed o, exactly as in ônibus.

grammar.title: Suggestions and advice
grammar.explanation:
A suggestion or a piece of advice asks the listener to act, so the rule of politeness applies: the more direct the wording, the stronger the pressure. Portuguese offers a ladder of patterns, from the softest to the firmest. The softest ask a question that is not really a question. Por que você não pede ajuda? is literally for-what you not ask help, the same device as English Why don't you ask for help? The verb is in the present, and the speaker does not want a reason. Que tal plus an infinitive or a noun means how about: Que tal sair mais cedo? Que tal um café? (Que is what and tal is such, so the phrase asks what do you think of such a thing.)

Next come the modal verbs, verbs that say what is possible or necessary: Você deveria descansar mais, Você devia descansar mais, Você poderia pedir um desconto. Dever is to owe, so deveria says you would owe it to yourself, as in English you ought to. The firmest pattern is Eu acho melhor plus an infinitive, literally I find better, that is, I think it is better: Eu acho melhor esperar. You can name the person who should act by putting the pronoun between melhor and the infinitive: Eu acho melhor você descansar um pouco. Keep that subject singular for now, because with a plural subject the infinitive takes an ending (the personal infinitive, a later topic). The last pattern is the formula from the previous note, Se eu fosse você, eu plus the conditional.

Note the spelling of por que. At the start of a question it is two words, por plus que, and it means why. The one-word porque means because, as in the answer. When the question ends with the word, it is written por quê, with a circumflex, because the que is now a stressed one-syllable word ending in e, and the stress rule from the second lesson requires an accent: Você saiu cedo. Por quê?

Two verbs recommend things: Eu recomendo and Eu sugiro, followed by a noun: Eu recomendo este hotel. Followed by a clause (Eu sugiro que você venha) they need the subjunctive, which comes later. Finally, Brazilians often soften advice with a tag: Você deveria descansar, né? Né is não é squeezed into one syllable, like English isn't it.

grammar.title: Probability: deve ser, será que, provavelmente
grammar.explanation:
English uses must to guess (He must be tired) as well as to oblige (You must study). Portuguese does the same with dever, and the resemblance has a reason. The basic meaning of dever is to owe (Eu devo dinheiro ao banco, I owe money to the bank). An obligation is something you owe, so Você deve estudar means you owe it to study, you must. A probability is something the facts owe, so Ele deve estar cansado means the facts owe him to be tired, he must be. Context decides which. When deve is followed by a state verb (ser, estar, ter) and the time is now, it is almost always probability: Deve ser difícil, Ela deve estar em casa, Ele deve ter uns trinta anos (uns is the plural of um, and before a number it means about). When it is followed by an action verb, obligation is the normal reading: Você deve estudar, Devo chegar mais cedo? (Should I arrive earlier?).

Será que builds a question from the future of ser: será is the future of ser, so será que is literally will-be that. The idea is the same in English, where the future is used to guess (That will be the postman): a future form points at something not yet known, and a guess about the present is the same kind of not yet known. Será que ele vem? therefore means I wonder if he is coming, a question put to yourself that does not demand an answer. Colloquially it is followed by the present or by vai plus infinitive, not by the simple future: Será que vai chover? Será que dá tempo? It is also a very polite way to open a request, because it turns the request into a wondering: Será que você poderia me ajudar?

Provavelmente (probably) and com certeza (for sure, literally with certainty) state how sure the speaker is, and together with deve they make a scale from the most to the least certain: com certeza, provavelmente, deve. The adverb provavelmente ends in -mente, like English -ly, and usually goes before the verb: Provavelmente vai chover à tarde. The word for perhaps, talvez, needs the subjunctive and comes later.

The simple future can also express probability about the present in formal or literary speech, as in Ele estará em casa agora. In everyday Brazilian speech people say Ele deve estar em casa.

grammar.title: Small words and idioms in the dialogues
grammar.explanation:
Several short expressions in this unit's dialogues are built from ordinary verbs used in a way English does not use them. Read each literally first, then as an idiom. Dar certo: dar is to give and certo is right, so dar certo is literally to give right, and it means to work out, to turn out well: Será que vai dar certo? The subject is the plan or the thing, not a person. Ter razão is literally to have reason and means to be right: Você tem razão. English uses be for this; Portuguese uses ter, the verb of having, as in tenho fome and tenho trinta anos.

Dá pra is the spoken form of dá para. Dá is the present of dar, here in the sense it gives, it allows, and pra is para shortened in speech, so Dá pra tomar café antes? is literally gives for to-take coffee before, and it means is it possible to have breakfast before? Mesmo after a pronoun works like English -self: eu mesmo is literally I same, and it means I myself. It agrees with the person, so a woman says eu mesma. Mesmo is also the common word for really and even. Pronto is ready, and it is the usual way to say done or there you go when something is finished: Pronto, está agendado. Está agendado is estar plus agendado, a word made from the verb agendar plus -ado, as cansado is made from cansar. It describes the resulting state, booked, and like an adjective it agrees in gender and number (agendada, agendados). The full system of these words comes in a later unit.

Finally, cedo is early. It is an adverb, so it never changes: mais cedo is earlier (literally more early) and amanhã cedo is early tomorrow. Tomar café is literally to take coffee, and Brazilians say take rather than drink for coffee; tomar café can also mean to have breakfast, and the full phrase is tomar café da manhã.

culture.title: Politeness, plans and the Brazilian future
culture.text:
Brazilians are warm, but in service situations they value polite wording, and the politeness is built into the grammar you have just studied. Gostaria de, poderia and por gentileza (literally for kindness) are standard with strangers, and in shops and cafes you will hear eu queria all the time, which is a softer imperfect form rather than a blunt statement of wants. A receptionist might say A senhora poderia aguardar um momento?, and a customer answers Claro, sem problema. Using o senhor (literally the gentleman) or a senhora (the lady) with older people and strangers is also a form of politeness, and a hotel clerk will keep it up even when you speak informally.

Talk about the future is often soft and flexible. Se Deus quiser, literally if God wishes, is added to many plans even by people who are not especially religious; quiser is a form of the future subjunctive of querer, which you will study later, so treat the whole phrase as one unit. Daqui a pouco, literally from-here to little, means in a little while but can be five minutes or two hours, and já já, literally already already, means very soon, with the same flexibility. When a Brazilian says Vamos marcar um dia (let's mark a day) or A gente se fala (literally the people talk to each other, meaning we will talk), it is often a friendly goodbye rather than a firm plan, so a clear follow-up like Que tal sábado às duas? is how you turn it into a real appointment. For doctor and dentist appointments, called consultas, being on time is expected, and clinics usually confirm by phone or WhatsApp the day before.

exercises.prompt: Match the future form with its meaning
Match the expression with its word-for-word meaning
Why does 'falará' carry a written accent while 'falarei' does not?
choices: Falará is plural and falarei is singular.
Both are stressed on the last syllable, but that breaks the default for an ending in a, while it is the default for ei.
The accent in falará marks a nasal vowel.
exercises.explanation: An accent appears when the stress disagrees with the default for the ending. The default for a is the second to last syllable, so stress on the last one needs the acute; the default for ei is the last syllable.

exercises.prompt: To what are the simple future endings added?
choices: The whole infinitive, including the -r
The stem, after removing -ar, -er or -ir
The eu form of the present
exercises.explanation: The future comes from the infinitive plus the present of haver: falar hei became falarei. That is why comer gives comerei and not comei.

exercises.prompt: Which statement about the simple future of 'ser', 'ter' and 'ir' is true?
choices: They lose a syllable, like fazer, dizer and trazer.
They have no simple future and use ir plus infinitive only.
They are regular: the infinitive plus the ending gives serei, terei and irei.
exercises.explanation: Only fazer, dizer and trazer are shortened. Every other verb keeps the full infinitive.

exercises.prompt: Which is the most common way to say 'I am going to travel next month' in spoken Brazilian Portuguese?
choices: Viajarei no mês que vem.
Vou viajar no mês que vem.
Viajei no mês que vem.
exercises.explanation: In speech, ir plus infinitive is the default way to talk about the future. The simple future sounds formal or written, and viajei is the past.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'gostaríamos' have a written accent when 'gostaria' does not?
choices: The extra syllable moves the stress to the third to last syllable, which no ending predicts, so an accent is required.
Every plural verb form carries an accent.
The accent shows a nasal vowel.
exercises.explanation: Gos-ta-RI-a is stressed on the second to last syllable, the default for a. Gos-ta-RÍ-a-mos is stressed on the third to last, so the accent is required, as in comíamos.

exercises.prompt: In 'When I was a child, I would play outside', which Portuguese form translates 'would play'?
choices: brincaria, the conditional
brincarei, the simple future
brincava, the imperfect
exercises.explanation: Here would means used to, a past habit, and habits are the job of the imperfect. The conditional is for imagined situations and polite wishes.

exercises.prompt: The basic meaning of 'dever' is 'to owe'. In which sentence does it express probability?
choices: Eu devo dinheiro ao banco.
Você deve estudar mais.
Ele deve estar cansado.
exercises.explanation: Deve followed by a state verb such as estar is a guess about the present: he must be tired. Devo dinheiro is owing money, and deve estudar is an obligation.

exercises.prompt: Which form follows 'será que' in everyday speech?
choices: The simple future, as in choverá
The present or vai plus infinitive, as in vai chover
The conditional, as in choveria
exercises.explanation: Será que already contains the future of ser, so the clause after it uses the ordinary spoken forms: Será que vai chover?

exercises.prompt: Why do we say 'Se eu fosse você, eu aceitaria' and not '... eu aceitarei'?
choices: In an imagined situation the result is also imagined, so it takes the conditional, while the future would present it as an expected fact.
Aceitarei is not a real word.
The simple future is used only in writing.
exercises.explanation: Fosse creates the imagined world and the conditional says what would happen in it. The simple future would state what will happen.

exercises.prompt: In 'Se eu fosse você', what is 'fosse'?
choices: The conditional of ser
The imperfect subjunctive of ser, used for imagined situations
The preterite of ir
exercises.explanation: Fosse is a subjunctive form, the mood for what is imagined or wished for. English keeps a trace of it in If I were you.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'provavelmente' have no written accent although 'provável' does?
choices: It is not stressed on any syllable.
In an adverb in -mente the main stress is on men, and the adjective's written accent is dropped.
Adverbs never carry accents.
exercises.explanation: Pro-va-vel-MEN-te has its main stress on men, so the written accent of provável is dropped, as in fácil and facilmente.

exercises.prompt: Why is 'disponível' written with an accent?
choices: Its stress is on the second to last syllable, but an ending in l expects the last syllable.
It is stressed on the third to last syllable.
The accent marks a nasal vowel.
exercises.explanation: Dis-po-NÍ-vel breaks the default for l, which is last syllable stress, so the stressed vowel takes an accent. The plural disponíveis keeps it.

Por que você pediu um desconto?
Você não pediu desconto.
exercises.explanation: Por que você não plus a present verb suggests an action, like English Why don't you ask for a discount? The past tense form asks for a reason.
